title: DeepSeek's cheap V4.1 Flash model undercuts the AI spending panic
summary: DeepSeek launches V4.1 Flash model to undercut rising AI infrastructure spending costs
detailed: While more than a trillion dollars evaporated from chip stocks this month on fears that AI spending won't pay off, DeepSeek quietly shipped a model that runs circles around that premise.
V4.1 Flash is fast, it's cheap, and it just became the top-ranked open-weight model on a major third-party leaderboard.
DeepSeek released V4.1 Flash, dated with the build tag 1017, in mid-October, and it has spent the weeks since climbing usage and consistency rankings on independent leaderboards.

V4.1 Flash is fast, it's cheap, and it just became the top-ranked open-weight model on a major third-party leaderboard.
DeepSeek released V4.1 Flash, dated with the build tag 1017, in mid-October, and it has spent the weeks since climbing usage and consistency rankings on independent leaderboards.
On BenchLM's tracker, the model now sits at the top of all open-weight models with a score of 65.2, ahead of DeepSeek's own V4 Pro at 62.5 and V3.2 at 49.7.
On OpenRouter, developers actually pay to run it.

There, V4.1 Flash is priced from $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens during off-peak hours, roughly double that at peak times, with cached reads costing a fraction of standard rates.
That is a fraction of what Anthropic charges for Claude Opus 4.6, which runs $5 and $25 per million tokens for input and output respectively.
Nvidia and the rest of the chip trade just went through one of the roughest stretches of the year.

The PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 10.3% in a single stretch, its worst showing since March 2020, and more than $1 trillion in market value disappeared within the first two hours of trading on the worst day.
Nvidia alone shed roughly 6% and over $300 billion in a session.
A Bank of America survey of 172 global fund managers found that 53% now believe AI stocks are in a bubble.
A net 20% say companies are overinvesting in AI capital spending, the first time that view has held a majority in two decades.
Here's the tension those investors are grappling with.
The entire bull case for Nvidia rests on the idea that frontier AI will keep needing exponentially more compute.
So does the case for the hundreds of billions in planned data centre buildouts behind it.
DeepSeek's newest model argues the opposite.
V4.1 Flash is a sparse mixture-of-experts system built around a 552 billion-parameter backbone, a 1 million token context window, and support for up to 384,000 tokens of output.
It's the first DeepSeek release built on what the company calls a Causal Encoder-Decoder architecture.
DeepSeek says it beats V4 Pro on performance, speed, and task completion time, despite sitting in the cheaper tier of the V4.1 family.

Independent benchmarking from Artificial Analysis puts its output speed above 200 tokens per second with a time to first token of just over one second, fast enough to rank near the top for open-weight intelligence without the usual speed tradeoff.

None of this happened in a vacuum.
DeepSeek's V4-generation models were built to run on Huawei's Ascend chips rather than Nvidia's.

According to reporting reviewed by multiple outlets covering the launch, DeepSeek-V4-Pro needs only 27% of the single-token inference compute and 10% of the key-value cache size that V3.2 required to handle a one-million-token context.

Huawei's Ascend hardware is the chip DeepSeek-V4 was built to run on, positioned as a domestic alternative to Nvidia's H20, the export-compliant chip Nvidia built specifically to keep selling into China under U.S. restrictions.
Put those pieces together and you get a company squeezing more intelligence out of cheaper chips.
Then it passes the savings straight into API pricing that undercuts GPT-5 and Claude by a factor of ten to twenty on output tokens, depending on which tier you compare.
The AI capex bulls have always needed one assumption to hold: that serving frontier-quality intelligence requires buying ever more GPUs, forever.
DeepSeek's actual, measured usage numbers suggest inference costs are falling faster than that assumption allows.
They are falling because of smarter architecture and cheaper hardware, not because anyone discovered a shortcut around physics.
That doesn't mean Nvidia's order book disappears.
Frontier labs in the US are still racing to pretrain ever-larger models, and training compute demand hasn't gone anywhere.
But V4.1 Flash is a live, usage-ranked counterexample to the idea that only the most expensive GPUs can produce a model good enough to matter.
A reader worried about their portfolio's AI exposure doesn't need to take DeepSeek's word for the efficiency story.
They can check the leaderboard themselves, and check the price.
